title: Signs in nature
hookLine: the camel, the bee, the ant, the spider, rain, stars: nature as a book of signs

lines: WILL THEY NOT REGARD THE CAMELS?
cards: "Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" That's surah eighty-eight, in Pickthall's translation.
Its first hearers rode camels, traded with them, drank their milk, and knew every habit and every sound they made. The question doesn't point them to a vision, or a miracle, or a far-off sky.
It points to the animal kneeling at the edge of the tent. Look at that, it says. Look at the thing you see every day.

teach.h: AYAH: A VERSE, AND A SIGN.
teach.b: The word the Qur'an keeps using for this is ayah. It's the word for a verse of the Qur'an. But it also means a sign, a mark that points beyond itself.
The same word names a line of scripture and a sunset. Then the book fills a whole zoo with it.

teach.h: THE BEE, THE ANT, THE SPIDER, THE RAIN.
teach.b: Several surahs carry animal names: the Cow, the Bee, the Ant, the Spider, the Elephant. The bee is inspired by its Lord to build homes in hills and trees and bring out a drink of many colors.
An ant calls out a warning to its colony so they won't be crushed, and a prophet smiles at it. The spider's house is called the frailest of houses. Rain comes down on dead ground and brings it back.
Stars are set for travelers to find their way by in the dark.
And again and again, a passage like these ends with a phrase like: in this are signs for people who reflect, or who use their reason, or who listen.
In surah three, the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the night and day taking turns, are signs for people of understanding.

Some Muslim thinkers put it this way: there are two books open at once, the written one and the created one, and each helps you read the other. In these passages, noticing the world isn't a distraction from faith.
The book keeps sending its listeners back outside.

how: Muslims call each verse of the Qur'an an ayah, a sign, and the same word is used for the signs in creation; reflection on nature (tafakkur) is a long-standing devotional practice.

games.q: you're a desert herder hearing surah eighty-eight. what does it ask you to look at?
o: the camels, how they are created.
the walls of a great city.
games.why: the camels: an everyday animal they knew well, held up as a sign.

practice: Take a slow walk outside, or sit by a window, and let your eyes stop on one living thing: an ant on the pavement, a bird, a tree, a cloud, a weed in a crack.
How is it made, what does it need, what is it doing right now without any help from you? Read it the way you'd read a line of a verse.

wordCard.voice: Ayah. The Qur'an's word for both a verse and a sign: camels, bees, ants, spiders, rain and stars, all pointing beyond themselves. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a sign; also a verse of the Qur'an.

carryVoice: Your line: the world is signs. Two books open at once, as some Muslim thinkers put it. See you tomorrow.
